name: Oxymetazoline eye drops (Upneeq)

lead: Upneeq is oxymetazoline hydrochloride 0.1% ophthalmic solution, approved by the FDA in July 2020 for acquired blepharoptosis in adults. For looks, it gives a brief lift to a mildly drooping upper lid so the eyes appear more open and awake.

Oxymetazoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist developed in 1961 and long used in nasal decongestant sprays and redness drops. For ptosis it is thought to stimulate receptors in Muller's muscle, which raises the lid. Published case reports also describe it for lid ptosis after botulinum toxin treatment.

paras: It is used as a prescription eye drop for a temporary lift that lasts for hours rather than a permanent change. On looksmax.org, users note it is costly and hard to obtain outside the US, and some ask whether nasal spray can substitute; nasal spray is made for the nose and is not the approved eye product.

Nasal oxymetazoline is described as causing rebound congestion and dependence. Clinicians' views on putting nasal spray in the eye are not covered here, and substituting it is not the approved use, so a clinician is the right person to ask.

chain: Eyes look more open and awake
angle.text: Upneeq is a prescription oxymetazoline eye drop that stimulates the lid muscle to lift a slightly drooping upper lid, so the eyes look more open and awake for a few hours. It is approved for acquired ptosis, and the lift has been studied in ptosis trials. Forum users also discuss nasal-spray substitutes, which are not the approved product.

lead: Upneeq is a brand of 0.1% oxymetazoline hydrochloride ophthalmic solution, approved by the US FDA in July 2020 to treat acquired blepharoptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid).[1] Oxymetazoline is an imidazole-derivative alpha-adrenergic agonist developed from xylometazoline at Merck in 1961, and is also used in nasal sprays, redness drops and a rosacea cream.[1]

For ptosis, the drug is thought to act on alpha receptors in Muller's muscle to lift the lid.[1] It is also used, in published case reports, to manage eyelid ptosis after botulinum toxin treatment.[2]
In looksmaxxing forums, Upneeq is discussed as a way to get a more open eye without surgery, and users discuss its cost and availability outside the US.[3]

paras: Approved use is acquired blepharoptosis in adults.[1] Published reports describe oxymetazoline 0.1% together with pretarsal botulinum toxin for severe botulinum-induced ptosis.[2] Wikipedia lists other oxymetazoline uses as nasal decongestion, eye redness and facial redness in rosacea.[1]
Oxymetazoline mainly activates alpha-1 and partly alpha-2 adrenergic receptors; in ptosis these actions in Muller's muscle are thought to elevate the lid.[1]

For nasal oxymetazoline, Wikipedia reports rebound congestion and describes a moderate dependence liability, with a 2006 review recommending limiting nasal use to three days.[1] Ophthalmic adverse-event data were not found in the sources reviewed.

A looksmax.org poster said that Upneeq is very expensive and nearly impossible to obtain in Europe, and asked whether a nasal spray seen used as eye drops on Reddit could serve as an alternative and whether this would be safe.[3]

Registered trials include a completed Phase 4 study of Upneeq on eyelid position, eye redness and appearance (NCT04831047, 114 participants),[4] a completed Phase 3 trial of oxymetazoline for ptosis from synkinesis (NCT05945615, 36 participants),[5] and a planned Phase 4 comparison of Upneeq and Lumify for ptosis (NCT07390578).[6] A published report describes oxymetazoline for botulinum-induced ptosis.[2]

lore.intro: Discussion centres on cost, availability and whether nasal sprays can be substituted.[3]

claims.claim: A nasal spray can be used as an alternative to Upneeq eye drops.

timeline.event: Oxymetazoline is developed at Merck (per Wikipedia).[1]
FDA approves 1% oxymetazoline cream for rosacea (per Wikipedia).[1]
FDA approves oxymetazoline 0.1% ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis.[1]
